ideas.a: It pumps blood out round the whole body (the systemic circuit)
It has the most muscular wall of the four, as it pumps blood the furthest
Blood comes into it from the atrium above through the bicuspid valve

model: The lower heart pump with the most muscular wall; it gets blood through the bicuspid valve and pumps it round the whole body.

ideas.a: It sits between the atrium and the ventricle (on the right side)
It shuts when the ventricle contracts, so blood can't flow back into the atrium
It is on the side carrying deoxygenated blood from the body
Its cusps are held in place by tendons (heart strings)

model: A one-way door between the atrium and ventricle on the deoxygenated side; it shuts when the ventricle contracts so blood can't flow back into the atrium.

ideas.a: Found at the base of the arteries leaving the ventricles (aorta and pulmonary artery)
It shuts when the ventricles relax, so blood can't flow back into them
Its cusps are shaped like half-moon pockets, with no tendons
Its closing makes the second heart sound ('dub')

model: Pocket-like flaps at the base of each artery leaving the ventricles; they shut when the ventricles relax, stopping blood flowing back into them.

ideas.a: It is in the wall of the right atrium
It starts each heartbeat and sets the heart rate
It sends out electrical signals that spread across the atria and make them contract

model: A patch of special tissue in the wall of the right atrium that sends electrical signals to start each beat and set the heart rate.

ideas.a: It carries blood away from the heart, out of the right ventricle
It goes to the lungs, where the blood picks up oxygen
Its blood is deoxygenated: the only artery like this

model: Takes oxygen-poor blood away from the heart's lower right chamber to the air sacs, where it can pick up oxygen.

ideas.a: It comes from the lungs
It brings blood back to the heart, into the left atrium
Its blood is oxygenated: the only vein with blood this rich in oxygen

model: Brings oxygen-rich blood from the air sacs back to the heart; the only one of its kind carrying blood this rich in oxygen.

ideas.a: It supplies the heart muscle itself with oxygen and food
It branches off the aorta and runs over the surface of the heart
If it is blocked (fatty deposits or a clot), part of the heart dies: a heart attack

model: Branches off the aorta and runs over the surface of the pumping organ, feeding its cardiac wall with oxygen; if it gets blocked, that tissue dies.

ideas.a: It starts at the small intestine (the villi)
It goes to the liver
Its blood is rich in absorbed food, like glucose and amino acids

model: Carries blood rich in absorbed food, like glucose, from the villi of the gut straight to the organ that stores glycogen and makes bile.

ideas.a: It carries oxygen, using haemoglobin (which contains iron)
It has no nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin
It is a biconcave disc, flexible enough to squeeze through capillaries

model: A disc dented on both sides with no nucleus, packed with an iron-rich pigment that carries oxygen round the body.

ideas.a: They help the blood to clot, sealing a cut to stop bleeding
They are fragments of bigger cells
They are made in the bone marrow

model: Tiny bits broken off bigger cells in the bone marrow; at a cut they stick together and form a plug to stop bleeding.

ideas.a: It carries blood back to the heart
Blood in it is under low pressure, so it has a thin wall and a wide lumen
It has valves (flaps) that stop blood flowing backwards
Blood is pushed along it by the squeezing of the muscles around it

model: A vessel bringing blood back to the heart at low pressure; it has a thin wall, a wide lumen and flaps inside that stop blood flowing the wrong way.

ideas.a: Its wall is only one cell thick
It links arterioles to venules (between arteries and veins)
Substances diffuse between the blood and the cells through tissue fluid
It is the narrowest vessel: red cells pass through in single file

model: The narrowest vessel, with a wall one cell thick, linking arterioles to venules; food and oxygen diffuse out of it into tissue fluid.

ideas.a: It is a phase of each heartbeat (the cardiac cycle)
The heart muscle contracts, pushing blood out of the chambers
It gives the higher blood pressure reading (e.g. the 120 in 120/80)

model: The phase of each beat when the heart muscle tightens, pushing blood out of the chambers into the arteries; pressure is at its peak then.

ideas.a: A wave of pressure that stretches the wall of an artery
There is one each time the left ventricle contracts (each heartbeat)
It is felt where an artery runs near the skin over a bone
It is counted per minute: about 72 at rest

model: The surge you feel where an artery runs near the skin, as its wall stretches each time the heart's ventricles contract; about 72 a minute at rest.

ideas.a: The force the blood puts on the walls of the vessels (arteries)
It is given as two numbers: systolic over diastolic, e.g. 120/80
It is measured with an arm cuff (a sphygmomanometer), in mmHg
It falls as the blood moves on through the capillaries to the veins

model: How hard the flowing liquid pushes against the walls of the vessels; read with an arm cuff as two numbers, like 120 over 80.

ideas.a: It collects the extra tissue fluid and returns it to the blood
It fights infection: its nodes filter out germs and hold lymphocytes
It absorbs fats from the small intestine (the lacteals in the villi)
It includes organs such as the spleen, tonsils and thymus

model: Vessels that collect excess tissue fluid and return it to the blood; on the way it passes through glands full of lymphocytes that trap germs.
